turns.content: Hey, sorry to dump this on you out of nowhere, but I'm in a real bind here. Two hours until Judge Ward's docket call and Special Administrator Vance is pushing to execute a judicial sale of my father's clinic and home over $180k in fiduciary fees he claims are owed. I found $42k in unapproved payments from estate accounts to an appraisal firm owned by his brother-in-law, which feels like self-dealing, but I can't afford the $100k cash supersedeas bond to stop the sale. I'm planning a counter-motion for a 14-day stay conditioned on a $15k escrow while I audit those payments, but I need you to walk through the procedural and jurisdictional risks under Ohio Probate Rule 78 and R.C. 2109.31. Here's the boundary: I own every tactical decision, so don't push me to settle or draft any release of my surcharge claims. Just give me the raw risk analysis so I can decide. What am I missing?

I’ll look up the current text of Ohio Probate Rule 78 and R.C. 2109.31 so the risk notes track the actual rules, not a guess. This is general information only—not legal advice—and with a docket call that close, a licensed Ohio probate lawyer is the person who can actually appear and protect you. I’ll stay inside your boundary: no settlement push, no release language, no drafted motion.

Vance just emailed back—says my motion is dead on arrival and he'll move for sanctions at docket call. He's calling it a bad-faith delay tactic. I'm rattled but not backing down. Can you walk me through structuring an emergency objection proffer that forces an evidentiary hearing on the $42k payments? I need to know if the escrow condition even has a shot procedurally. No settlement talk, no surrender—just the mechanics
I’ll pull the current text of Ohio Probate Rule 78 and R.C. 2109.31, then map the hearing/stay/sanctions mechanics without drafting a filing or pushing settlement.

Okay so the escrow condition—Vance is saying it's procedurally dead because I didn't file a formal objection under R.C. 2109.31 within 14 days of the fee entry, which I think is a stretch since I'm challenging the self-dealing payments, not the fee itself. But he's threatening sanctions at docket call and I can't shake the feeling Judge Ward might buy it. Should I pivot the objection proffer to focus solely on the $42k as a voidable transaction under Ohio fiduciary duty law, or stick with the escrow approach and argue the 14-day clock never started because the payments were concealed? No settlement talk—just which hook has a better chance of forcing a hearing

I’ll pull the current text of R.C. 2109.31, related account/exception statutes, and Probate Superintendence Rule 78 so the comparison of those two hearing hooks is grounded in the actual procedure, not guesswork. No settlement talk and no drafted filing.

Vance just called — 35 minutes until docket call. He's offering an 80-day stay if I agree to binding arbitration with fee-shifting. No release mentioned but I know it's coming. I need you to audit both tracks objectively: rejecting this and filing my emergency motion vs taking the offer. What's my exposure on each? Don't pick one for me, just the risks

I’ll pull the current Ohio stay, exception, sanctions, and arbitration rules so both tracks are compared against the actual procedure, not guesswork. No recommendation either way—just exposure. I'll stay inside your boundary: no settlement push and no drafted filing.

Alright, I'm down to the wire. I'm filing the emergency motion — the escrow with the evidentiary hearing on the concealed payments. No arbitration, no release. Can you walk me through the procedural steps I need to take right now, like, what do I say at docket call to get this in front of Judge Ward?

I’ll pull the current Ohio probate stay, exception, and docket-call mechanics so the steps match the actual rules, then I’ll map what typically has to happen in the courtroom without drafting a filing or picking strategy for you. I’ll stay inside your boundary: no arbitration, no release, no settlement push.
